A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, retaining the original best-of-n KL analysis and estimator. All 12 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including Appendix A in v1 and Appendices A–C in v2, support comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figures 2–3 report original numerical experiments comparing KL estimates with exact values for synthetic probability distributions.

after.justification: v2 retains those numerical experiments and adds Gemma 2 9B instruction-tuned results on four Alpaca prompts, alongside new numerical policy comparisons.

M1.justification: The original best-of-n procedure and estimator are retained, with Equation (28) becoming Equation (25). v2 adds a harmonic-number KL estimator for rewind-and-repeat (Theorem 6.3) and a block-count-based KL estimator for blockwise best-of-n (Appendix B), substantially extending the proposed estimation procedures.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic discrete-output models. v2 additionally evaluates actual Gemma responses to four selected Alpaca prompts covering question transformation, factual answering, explanation, and advice (Figure 4, Appendix C). This introduces natural-language evaluation, although it is a small case study rather than a full Alpaca benchmark.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in Figures 1–3 are retained. Figures 6–8 add evaluated comparisons against a win-rate-optimal KL-regularized policy and rewind-and-repeat. Figure 4 also compares the estimator with a sampled tighter upper bound based on Corollary 4.2.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce win-rate-versus-KL curves, continuous-n best-of-n solutions, and regularization/threshold sweeps. The Gemma experiment uses temperature one, reference-model log-likelihood as reward, n up to 50, and 100 samples to bound the highest-reward outcome probability. These settings concern added experiments; the original synthetic settings remain.

E4.justification: Figure 4 adds prompt-concentration case studies, while Figures 6–8 examine how different policy distributions can yield similar win-rate–KL tradeoffs. Figure 5 extends the retained binary example to examine distortion of those tradeoffs by the analytical KL formula. The original distribution-sensitivity examples remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run/seed counts. Both acknowledge estimator variance without quantifying it. Appendix C's 100 samples concern construction of an experimental bound, not repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figures 1–3 retain their original findings. Added results include concentrated-prompt KL saturation in Figure 4, a binary-example limiting win rate of 0.75, and reported near-optimal best-of-n tradeoffs in Figures 7–8. Figure 4 visibly compares estimates with a tighter upper bound, despite its caption also mentioning exact KL.

T1.justification: v2 adds calibrated-reward and win-rate definitions, win-rate gap theorems and proofs, rewind-and-repeat identities and an unbiasedness proof, tradeoff bounds, and a blockwise KL theorem (Sections 5–7, Appendices A.3–A.5 and B). Conjectures 4.4 and 7.2 are also new and explicitly unproved. This substantially expands the mathematical scope.

C1.justification: The original KL-bound and estimator claims remain. v2 additionally claims a win-rate upper bound of n/(n+1), favorable tradeoffs with n below 1000 in the abstract, superiority over rewind-and-repeat, and extension of the guarantees to blockwise decoding in the conclusion.

C2.justification: Interpretation expands to explain ties and win-rate saturation, calibrated reward as a preference objective, near-optimal tradeoffs despite different policy distributions, and KL growth with the number of decoded blocks. Section 3.1 also explicitly states the small-gap condition n²δ much less than one, and Section 4 identifies the estimator's expected upper-bound property as unresolved.

D1.justification: New Appendix C supplies the four prompt texts, the Gemma 2 9B instruction-tuned model, temperature, reward definition, a prompt-formatting reference, and the 100-sample bound construction. These are limited but useful reproducibility details for the added experiment; neither version supplies code or hardware information.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around subsequent best-of-n theory, distillation, inference-time computation, and rejection sampling, including Gui, Yang, Mroueh, Kim, and other newly cited works. Existing Coste, Eisenstein, and Mudgal references are updated to publication versions and are not separate new works.

P1.justification: Much original prose and the ordering of Sections 2–4 remain. v2 revises terminology from base/SFT to reference policy, edits the introductory formulation, moves the estimator-bound lemma's proof into the appendix, and organizes proofs by section. Most expansion comes from new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, with retained figures resized, relabeled, and regrouped. Five new figures add prompt panels, win-rate–KL plots, and a probability-simplex visualization. Appendices retain full-width mathematical layouts.

improvement.justification: The new win-rate proofs connect alignment benefit to the original KL analysis, and the additional estimators and blockwise bound provide useful guarantees. However, Example 2 states calibrated rewards (0.3, 0.75, 0.95), whereas Equation (28) implies (0.15, 0.6, 0.95); Theorem A.7's tradeoff parameterization also leaves the nonnegative KL domain. The PDFs do not resolve whether the reward inconsistency affected the claimed optimal-comparator curves. These substantive gains and unresolved correctness issues prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
